rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Referent resolution under a sequential deck read.
rules_evaluated.evidence: chunk 5 line 43 'the orient, fix, compound, close loop' is host-module spine vocabulary: getting-going.md (M1's module file, which includes this lecture last) names 'The loop is orient → fix → compound → close' in its own Key Concepts and builds the What You'll Learn LOs around Run/Introspect/Fix/Compound — module-include-order prior context, not a fresh forward reference. chunk 5's eight-token Klaassen sequence ('ideate → brainstorm → plan → work → review → polish → compound → repeat') is likewise not novel at this point in the deck: compound-and-close.md (M1 Ex3, immediately preceding this lecture) already prints the identical arrow-sequence verbatim in its own 'The point:' line, so the closing slide is a callback to something the student read minutes earlier, not an unexplained import. chunk 4's 'the workbook' resolves against getting-going.md's own prework pointer, same host module. No pronoun or demonstrative anywhere in the body fails to resolve under the sequential read once host-module signposting is checked.

chunk 5's 'The story of building this training is the shape you just ran on your own repo' is a closer summing its own deck (this file's own chunks 0-4), matching the compendium's own worked PASS example for this exact line. No positional pointer at another file by position anywhere in the body.

rules_evaluated.evidence: chunk 5's backward beats ('you let Claude read your repo, saw the wrongness, named it, corrected it', 'the retro you just ran') resolve against orient-and-introspect.md, fix-tests-first.md/diagnose-and-resend.md, and compound-and-close.md — all current M1 exercises per getting-going.md's include order, confirmed against the module file directly.

rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Live-demo beats survive a text read.
rules_evaluated.evidence: No guess-before-reveal construction anywhere in the body; this is a narrative lecture, not an interactive demo beat.

chunk 5 header 'You just ran the compound loop' still holds against its body: the body affirms one loop under two names ('the names differ, the loop doesn't') rather than contradicting the header's singular claim. All other headers match their chunk content directly.

chunk 5 "You just ran the compound loop": line 43: "The retro you just ran was the compound step of his loop: ideate → brainstorm → plan → work → review → polish → compound → repeat. That is the orient, fix, compound, close loop cut at different joints; the names differ, the loop doesn't." — sub-item 'Number + own retraction', generalized from a single number to a sequence-count: this is the module's closing slide, and it prints Klaassen's eight-token arrow-sequence in full, then immediately asks the reader to reconcile it against the training's own four-token loop with a bare assertion rather than a shown mapping. Same shape the rule bans for a hedged percentage, applied here to a hedged headcount ('the names differ, the loop doesn't' functions exactly like 'could be more, could be less'). Both sequences are independently earned earlier in the module's own deck order (getting-going.md names the four-step loop; compound-and-close.md, the exercise immediately prior, already prints the identical eight-token quote), so this is not a referent-novelty problem — it is a density problem: two differently-sized taxonomies asserted equivalent on the one slide meant to leave the student with a single takeaway, at the exact point the training wants to land clean. Every other sub-item (banned triple construction, anaphora/epistrophe, self-grading superlatives, abstraction-noun stacks, empty-leg verb triplets) checked clean across all six chunks — chunk 1's 'Some were overscoped. Some fired on the wrong surface. Some held for one kind of content and broke for another' is a triple whose third leg carries new concrete content (content-type failure, distinct from breadth and placement) and passes the rule's own third-leg test.
rules_evaluated.fix_hint: Drop one of the two sequences from this slide — keep either the Klaassen quote or the orient/fix/compound/close restatement, not both reconciled by assertion, on the training's own closing beat.

rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Internal dialect never lands on a slide.
rules_evaluated.evidence: chunk 1 "Wrong is how steering gets in": line 13: "Some fired on the wrong surface." — two repo-internal dialect terms stacked in one clause: 'fired' (this repo's own rule-activation verb — content-rules.md's 'Fires when…', check_slides.md's own 'Fires per chunk') and 'surface' used as the noun this repo reserves for a content-context category (content-rules.md's 'Surface → compendium' routing table; check_slides.md §8 lists 'surface as noun' as its own canonical dialect example). A student with no access to the compendium/routing system cannot parse 'fired on the wrong surface' as 'applied to the wrong kind of writing' — it reads as an internal system term, not ordinary English. Not covered by either of the file's own documented maintainer exceptions (bold budget, size-gate exemption), and 'subagent'/'plan mode' (the terms the file's Register check note does carve out for AE101) are a different, already-licensed case.
rules_evaluated.fix_hint: Recast in plain English — e.g. 'applied to the wrong kind of writing' or 'used on content it wasn't meant for' — no compendium-routing vocabulary.
